## Research question

How did the percentage of Canadians reporting fruit and vegetable
consumption five or more times per day change between 2015 and 2021?

## Data source

The data come from Statistics Canada's
[Canadian Indicator Framework, indicator 3.1.1](https://sdgcif-data-canada-oddcic-donnee.github.io/3-1-1/).

This indicator measures how frequently people report eating fruits
and vegetables, not the number of servings or the amount consumed.

The data are available under the
[Statistics Canada Open Licence](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/terms-conditions/open-licence).

Adapted from Statistics Canada, Canadian Indicator Framework,
indicator 3.1.1, reference years 2015–2021. This does not constitute
an endorsement by Statistics Canada of this product.

## Python setup

I load the packages for the analysis and display the Python executable
to check which environment runs this post.

```{python}
#| label: setup-python
#| warning: false

import sys
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print(sys.executable)
```

## Load and inspect the data

I read the downloaded CSV and display it to check the column names
and available years before selecting the observations for this analysis.

```{python}
#| label: load-nutrition-data

nutrition_raw = pd.read_csv("data/fruit_vegetable_canada.csv")

nutrition_raw
```
## Prepare the data

I keep the available observations from 2015 through 2021 to match
my research question. I select the year and percentage, give the
percentage column a clearer name, and sort the observations by year.

```{python}
#| label: prepare-nutrition-data
#| echo: true

selected_years = (nutrition_raw["Year"] >= 2015) & (nutrition_raw["Year"] <= 2021)

nutrition = nutrition_raw.loc[selected_years, ["Year", "Value"]].copy()

nutrition = nutrition.rename(columns={"Value": "Percentage"})

nutrition = nutrition.sort_values("Year")

nutrition
```

The prepared data contain five observations. The downloaded dataset
has no observations for 2018 or 2019, so I leave those years missing
rather than treating them as zero. The empty GeoCode column is not
needed for this analysis.

## Calculate the change

I compare the first and last percentages in the prepared data.
Subtracting the 2015 percentage from the 2021 percentage gives
the change in percentage points.

```{python}
#| label: calculate-nutrition-change
#| echo: true

first_percentage = nutrition["Percentage"].iloc[0]
last_percentage = nutrition["Percentage"].iloc[-1]

change_pp = last_percentage - first_percentage

print(f"2015: {first_percentage:.1f}%")
print(f"2021: {last_percentage:.1f}%")
print(f"Change: {change_pp:.1f} percentage points")
```

The reported percentage decreased from 31.5% in 2015 to 21.8%
in 2021. This is a decrease of 9.7 percentage points, not a
9.7% relative decrease.

This calculation describes the difference between the published
estimates. It does not explain why the estimates changed.
## Visualize the trend

I plot the percentage for each available year. Each dot represents
a published observation. The connecting lines help show the pattern,
but they do not provide estimates for the missing years.

```{python}
#| label: fig-nutrition-python
#| fig-cap: "Percentage reporting fruit and vegetable consumption five or more times per day, Canada (excluding territories), available years from 2015 to 2021. Source: Statistics Canada."
#| fig-alt: "Five observations declining from 31.5% in 2015 to 21.8% in 2021, with no observations for 2018 or 2019."
#| echo: true

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))

plt.plot(
    nutrition["Year"],
    nutrition["Percentage"],
    marker="o"
)

plt.title("Fruit and vegetable consumption in Canada")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Reported percentage (%)")

plt.xticks(range(2015, 2022))
plt.ylim(0, 40)

plt.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Conclusion

The published percentage reporting fruit and vegetable consumption
five or more times per day decreased from 31.5% in 2015 to 21.8%
in 2021, a decline of 9.7 percentage points.

The percentage was lower at each successive observation in this
dataset. However, observations are missing for 2018 and 2019,
so the data do not show what happened in every individual year.

This is a descriptive comparison of published estimates, not a test
of statistical significance. The indicator measures reported eating
frequency rather than portion sizes or overall diet quality, and
this analysis does not establish why the estimates changed.
